newsitem.title: FRANCE: Elf refinery strike in fifth day as union aims widen.
newsitem.headline: Elf refinery strike in fifth day as union aims widen.

text.p: Striking oil workers halted Elf Aquitaine refineries for a fifth day on Monday as union leaders raised the stakes by demanding the same early retirement right just won by victorious French truckers.

Workers at Elf's three French refineries voted to extend into Tuesday a strike originally intended as a one-day protest over jobs but now billed by unions as a wider action against cost cutting by oil firms and government social policies.
"The truck strike was an early warning," said Claude Henry of the CFTC, strike coordinator at one the unions at Elf, France's largest oil firm.
"You get to a point where the only way to save money is on the backs of the employees, and there's no social protection. It has become impossible for everyone," he said.
Union officials said they aimed to put pressure on a centre-right government bruised by 12 days of road blockades and petrol rationing in the truckers' strike which ended on Friday.
But while several oil companies have had sporadic protests such as go-slows over the past two weeks, none reported signs that the Elf strike was spreading on Monday evening.
Unions said they were still holding shop-floor meetings at most plants to decide whether to take action for pay, earlier retirement, job security and other demands.
The stricken Elf plants include France's biggest refinery at Donges in western France as well as the Grandpuits refinery near Paris and the Feyzin refinery serving France's second city Lyon.

Together they make up a quarter of French capacity and three quarters of Elf's European refining network. But oil markets shrugged off the closures at a time when most refiners are struggling with surplus capacity.
Elf officials said there was no shortage of fuel since depots were mostly full in the wake of the truckers' blockade.
But industry sources said the strike would clearly hamper Elf's efforts to get back to normal after the truck strike brought nearly two weeks of havoc to French oil firms.
At issue is a plan by distribution subsidiary Elf Antar to shed 330 jobs, or about 10 percent of its workforce, to cope with fierce competition.
But echoing the truckers, unions said they also wanted talks over retirement at 55 instead of 60 for refinery shift workers.
However, many analysts say the refinery workers lack the truckers' power to paralyse France and win government-brokered concessions from the private sector.
Union officials accused Elf of refusing to negotiate over their wider demands and trying to confine the dispute to the narrow issue of pay. Some talks were scheduled for Tuesday.
Elf declined to comment on the strike.

Five unions called on Friday for protests at all French refineries about plans by several oil companies to slim down or merge their refining operations to recover from weak profit margins and strong retail competition.
French oil companies say their situation is particularly bad because of extra competition from supermarkets which control half the country's market for petrol.
